# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and other large-bore structural heart interventions are most commonly performed through transfemoral arterial access. However, a substantial minority of patients have iliofemoral arteries that are too small, calcified, tortuous, or diseased to accommodate large introducer sheaths. The transcaval (TCv) vascular approach is increasingly used in transcatheter aortic valve replacement in patients unsuitable for the gold-standard transfemoral approach [1]. Transcaval access offers a fully percutaneous, non-transthoracic route that avoids the morbidity historically associated with transapical and direct aortic approaches [2].

## Concept and Rationale

Transcaval access is fundamentally an electrosurgical technique. Transcaval aortic access is a versatile electrosurgical technique for large-bore arterial access through the wall of the abdominal aorta from the adjoining inferior vena cava. Although counterintuitive, its relative safety derives from the recognition that interstitial hydraulic pressure exceeds venous pressure, so arterial bleeding harmlessly decompresses into the nearby caval venous hole [3]. The technique relies on transcatheter electrosurgery, in which radiofrequency energy applied to the tip of an insulated guidewire vaporizes tissue to traverse the caval and aortic walls despite flowing blood [4].

The approach was first validated preclinically. Large therapeutic devices can be introduced into the aorta via the IVC in a simple catheter procedure, and the fistula closed uneventfully despite full anticoagulation. Intentional failure to close the caval-aortic access tract is well-tolerated and easily redressed [5]. These swine experiments established the safety rationale that subsequently enabled human translation.

## Procedural Technique

In practice, a catheter directs a transfemoral vein guidewire from the inferior vena cava towards a snare target positioned in the adjoining abdominal aorta; a catheter is advanced over the guidewire into the aorta and used to introduce a more rigid guidewire; the valve introducer sheath is advanced from the vena cava into the aorta; and after completion of TAVR, the aorto-caval access tract is closed with a nitinol occluder [6]. Detailed step-by-step technical guidance for access and closure has been published to facilitate dissemination [7]. Importantly, transcaval TAVR is logistically attractive: transcaval TAVR is readily performed using moderate sedation and has ergonomics indistinguishable from standard femoral access [8].

## Patient Selection and CT Planning

Candidate selection depends on cross-sectional imaging. A dedicated CT-based methodology teaches operators how to identify a suitable crossing target [9]. Candidates need a calcium-free window on the caval side of the aorta, away from important arterial branches, with no interposed viscerae, within reach of an available TAVR introducer sheath. Caval-aortic distance does not matter. Most patients who are ineligible for standard transfemoral access are eligible for transcaval access [9]. Esoteric obstacles such as IVC filters and even polyester aortic grafts have been managed, the latter traversed with radiofrequency energy [10,11].

## Clinical Evidence

The first-in-human experience demonstrated feasibility. Caval-aortic access and tract closure were successful in all 19 patients; TAVR was successful in 17 patients. Six patients experienced modified VARC-2 major vascular complications, 2 (11%) of whom required intervention. Most (79%) required blood transfusion. There were no deaths attributable to caval-aortic access [12].

A prospective, multicenter investigational device exemption study followed, enrolling 100 patients without good transthoracic options and using nitinol cardiac occluders off-label for closure [13]. The intermediate-term durability of the access tract was subsequently characterized in the 12-month NHLBI study, which used a prospective, multi-center, independently-adjudicated trial of transcaval access, using Amplatzer nitinol cardiac occluders, among subjects without traditional transthoracic access options, with one-year clinical follow-up including core laboratory analysis of serial abdominal CTs [14]. The European experience corroborated these findings: transcaval access was successful in 49 out of 50 patients and device success was obtained in 94% of cases; closure of the caval-aortic puncture site with a nitinol cardiac occluder was successful in all cases without need for emergent surgery [15]. Anatomic suitability analyses confirmed that most transfemoral-ineligible patients have a feasible transcaval window [16].

A persistent limitation has been bleeding, prompting development of a purpose-built closure device. In first-in-human testing, the primary endpoint of technical success was met in 100% of subjects, with complete closure achieved in 75% at exit from the catheterization lab and in 100% at 30 days, with no major vascular complications [17].

## Comparative Outcomes

Comparative data are encouraging. In a propensity-weighted analysis, stroke and transient ischemic attack were 5-fold less common after transcaval than transaxillary access (2.5% vs 13.2%) [18]. A subsequent meta-analysis of 8 studies including 467 patients reported a procedural success rate of 98.5% and 30-day all-cause mortality of approximately 6%, supporting transcaval access as a viable alternative [1,19]. Contemporary best-practice and consensus documents now position transcaval access alongside transaxillary and transcarotid routes within structural heart programs [3,20,21].

## Expanding Applications

Beyond TAVR, transcaval access has broadened to other large-bore needs. Transcaval aortic access has been used for deployment of transcatheter aortic valves in patients in whom conventional arterial approaches are not feasible; it has also been used for thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) in lieu of a surgical iliac conduit [22]. The technique has also enabled emergency mechanical circulatory support: transcaval access is feasible for emergency nonsurgical implantation of the Impella 5.0 device in cardiogenic shock with small or diseased iliofemoral arteries, allowing early institution of higher-flow MCS [23]. Related electrosurgical innovations have catalyzed an entire family of structural procedures [24], and transcaval access has even been described in congenital heart disease [25] and across previously placed aortic grafts [26].

## Conclusion

Transcaval access has matured from a counterintuitive concept into an established, fully percutaneous alternative for patients lacking suitable transfemoral or transthoracic options [27]. Its safety derives from sound physiologic principles, its outcomes compare favorably with other nonfemoral routes, and its applications continue to expand across structural and vascular interventions [28,29]. Wider adoption has historically been limited by the absence of commercially marketed dedicated devices, and ongoing device development together with randomized comparison would further define its role [30].
